title: RAMIPRIL capsules, for oral use: full prescribing information
journal: US Food and Drug Administration-approved labelling, published in DailyMed (National Library of Medicine); structured product label version 19, effective 18 September 2026, label text revised 09/2026
funder: not stated. The document is prescribing information approved by the US Food and Drug Administration and published by the labeller, Aurobindo Pharma Limited.
result: Initial US approval 1991. Indications: hypertension; reduction of the risk of myocardial infarction, stroke or death from cardiovascular causes in patients of 55 years or older at high risk; and heart failure after myocardial infarction. Boxed warning, fetal toxicity: when pregnancy is detected, discontinue as soon as possible; drugs that act directly on the renin-angiotensin system can cause injury and death to the developing fetus. Chemistry and metabolism: ramiprilat, the diacid metabolite, is a non-sulfhydryl ACE inhibitor; ramipril is converted to ramiprilat by hepatic cleavage of the ester group; ramipril is almost completely metabolised to ramiprilat, which has about 6 times the ACE inhibitory activity of ramipril, and to the inactive diketopiperazine ester, diketopiperazine acid and glucuronides. Pharmacokinetics: peak plasma concentrations of ramipril within 1 hour and of ramiprilat 2 to 4 hours after intake; extent of absorption at least 50% to 60%; absolute bioavailability 28% for ramipril and 44% for ramiprilat; serum protein binding about 73% and 56%; plasma ramiprilat declines triphasically, the initial distribution phase with a half-life of 2 to 4 hours, the apparent elimination phase of free ramiprilat 9 to 18 hours and a terminal phase above 50 hours that probably represents the binding and dissociation kinetics of the ramiprilat-ACE complex and does not contribute to accumulation; after multiple daily doses of 5 to 10 mg the half-life within the therapeutic range was 13 to 17 hours; steady state by the fourth dose; about 60% of parent drug and metabolites is eliminated in urine and about 40% recovered in faeces, with less than 2% of the dose recovered in urine as unchanged ramipril. Single doses of 2.5 to 20 mg inhibit plasma ACE activity by about 60% to 80% at 4 hours and 40% to 60% at 24 hours; multiple doses of 2 mg or more lower plasma ACE activity by more than 90% at 4 hours with over 80% inhibition remaining at 24 hours. Renal impairment: in a single-dose study the AUC(0-24h) for ramiprilat was about 1.7-fold, 3-fold and 3.2-fold higher with mild (creatinine clearance 40 to 80 ml/min), moderate (15 to 40 ml/min) and severe (below 15 ml/min) impairment than with normal renal function; in multiple-dose regimens total exposure to ramiprilat below 40 ml/min/1.73 m2 is 3 to 4 times as large as with normal renal function, and 25% of the usual dose is expected to produce full therapeutic levels of ramiprilat; in hepatic impairment metabolism to ramiprilat appears slowed and plasma ramipril levels are about 3-fold increased, while peak ramiprilat concentrations are unchanged. Mechanism: ACE, a peptidyl dipeptidase, catalyses the conversion of angiotensin I to the vasoconstrictor angiotensin II, which also stimulates adrenal aldosterone secretion; the enzyme is identical to kininase, which degrades bradykinin, and whether raised bradykinin plays a part in the therapeutic effect remains to be elucidated; removal of angiotensin II negative feedback raises plasma renin activity; the drug is antihypertensive even in low-renin hypertension, with a smaller average response in Black than in non-Black patients. Hyperkalaemia (serum potassium above 5.7 mEq/l) occurred in approximately 1% of hypertensive patients; in most cases these were isolated values that resolved despite continued therapy, and no patient was withdrawn for hyperkalaemia; risk factors are renal insufficiency, diabetes mellitus and concomitant drugs that raise serum potassium. Cough: persistent nonproductive cough has been reported with all ACE inhibitors, presumably caused by inhibition of the degradation of endogenous bradykinin, always resolving after discontinuation of therapy. In a later 1-year study increased cough was seen in almost 12% of patients, with about 4% requiring discontinuation. Angio-oedema is presumed to follow effects on the metabolism of eicosanoids and polypeptides, including endogenous bradykinin; in a large US post-marketing study angio-oedema was reported in 3 of 1523 (0.2%) Black and 8 of 8680 (0.09%) non-Black patients, rates that were not statistically different; angioneurotic oedema was reported in 0.3% of patients in US clinical trials. HOPE study, as described in this label: 9541 patients of 55 years or older at high cardiovascular risk, 4645 on ramipril 10 mg once daily, mean follow-up 5 years; the two group sizes given in the label's own table sum to 9297, the number randomised in the HOPE publication; myocardial infarction, stroke or death from cardiovascular causes in 651 of 4645 (14.0%) against 826 of 4652 (17.8%) on placebo (relative risk 0.78, 95% CI 0.70 to 0.86); death from cardiovascular causes 282 (6.1%) against 377 (8.1%) (0.74, 0.64 to 0.87); myocardial infarction 459 (9.9%) against 570 (12.3%) (0.80, 0.70 to 0.90); stroke 156 (3.4%) against 226 (4.9%) (0.68, 0.56 to 0.84); death from any cause 482 (10.4%) against 569 (12.2%) (0.84, 0.75 to 0.95). Reasons for stopping or interrupting treatment in HOPE, ramipril against placebo: cough 7% against 2%, hypotension or dizziness 1.9% against 1.5%, angio-oedema 0.3% against 0.1%. AIRE study: 2006 patients with clinical signs of heart failure 2 to 9 days after acute myocardial infarction, average follow-up 15 months (range 6 to 46 months); ramipril was associated with a 27% reduction in the risk of death from any cause (p=0.002), a 23% reduction in progression to severe heart failure (p=0.017) and a 26% reduction in heart failure-related hospitalisation (p=0.011); adverse reactions more frequent on ramipril included hypotension 11% against 5% and increased cough 8% against 4%. Dual blockade: in ONTARGET, 25,620 patients older than 55 years with atherosclerotic disease or diabetes with end-organ damage were randomised to telmisartan, ramipril or the combination and followed for a median 56 months; the combination gave no benefit for the composite of cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, stroke and heart failure hospitalisation and increased clinically important renal dysfunction, so concomitant use is not recommended. Abrupt withdrawal of ramipril has not resulted in a rapid increase in blood pressure. Patients are advised to report immediately any sign suggesting angio-oedema and to temporarily discontinue the drug until they have consulted the prescribing physician, and not to use potassium-containing salt substitutes without consulting their physician.
